evidence.claim: Switchbacks climb Pine Creek Canyon to a tunnel inside its rock wall
evidence.quote: The highway features a 5,613-foot (1,711 m) tunnel that follows the profile of the Pine Creek Canyon wall

evidence.claim: Switchbacks climb Pine Creek Canyon to a tunnel inside its rock wall
evidence.quote: continues up Pine Creek Canyon, up the switchbacks and into the Zion-Mt. Carmel Tunnel.

evidence.claim: SR 9 climbs past mesas and follows the Virgin River into Zion before switchbacks lift it into Pine Creek Canyon and the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel.
evidence.quote: After leaving La Verkin, SR-9 heads uphill and passes several mesas before eventually going through the small towns of Virgin, Rockville, and Springdale.

evidence.claim: SR 9 climbs past mesas and follows the Virgin River into Zion before switchbacks lift it into Pine Creek Canyon and the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel.
evidence.quote: The highway begins on the south side of Zion National Park following along the North Fork of the Virgin River. The road then turns at the junction of Pine Creek and the North Fork of the Virgin River and continues up Pine Creek Canyon, up the switchbacks and into the Zion-Mt. Carmel Tunnel.

evidence.claim: The whole highway is the Zion Park Scenic Byway; its SR 17–East Rim Trail Road section received national scenic designation in 2021.
evidence.quote: The entire length of the highway has been designated the Zion Park Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: its SR 17–East Rim Trail Road section received national scenic designation in 2021.
evidence.quote: (9) Zion National Scenic Byway (a) Comprised of the section of the Zion Park Scenic Byway starting at the intersection of SR-17 and SR-9 and ending at the intersection of SR-9 and East Rim Trail Road. (b) Designated National Scenic Byway January 19, 2021.

evidence.claim: Utah’s tourism office highlights the national byway’s scenery, communities and public-land recreation, while UDOT advises allowing at least an hour and a half.
evidence.quote: The Zion National Scenic Byway is a spectacular road that showcases unparalleled scenery, vibrant communities and diverse opportunities for outdoor recreation on public lands.

evidence.claim: UDOT advises allowing at least an hour and a half.
evidence.quote: Allow at least one-and-a-half hours for this drive.

evidence.claim: The eastern road made a regional park journey possible.
evidence.quote: The road became part of a loop tour of Zion, Bryce Canyon National Park, Cedar Breaks National Monument, and the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park.

evidence.claim: After considering alternatives, the National Park Service chose Pine Creek, a route requiring a tunnel through the Great Arch.
evidence.quote: The National Park Service evaluated alternative routes, including one that used Parunuweap Canyon (following the East Fork Virgin River), but settled on the Pine Creek route, which required a tunnel through the Great Arch.

evidence.claim: Work began in 1927 and finished in 1930, creating a road that joined a touring loop through Zion, Bryce Canyon, Cedar Breaks and the Grand Canyon’s North Rim.
evidence.quote: Work began in 1927 on a total of 25 miles (40 km) of road, which was completed in 1930.

evidence.claim: creating a road that joined a touring loop through Zion, Bryce Canyon, Cedar Breaks and the Grand Canyon’s North Rim.
evidence.quote: The road became part of a loop tour of Zion, Bryce Canyon National Park, Cedar Breaks National Monument, and the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Public Roads handled the detailed road design, while the Park Service designed bridges, retaining walls and culverts under Thomas Chalmers Vint.
evidence.quote: Detailed design work on the road was carried out by the Bureau of Public Roads. Details including bridges, retaining walls, culverts, and other features were designed by the National Park Service Branch of Plans and Design under the supervision of Thomas Chalmers Vint.

evidence.claim: From I-15, drive through Hurricane and La Verkin, then east through Virgin, Rockville and Springdale.
evidence.quote: SR-9 begins at I-15, Exit 16, at Harrisburg Junction

evidence.claim: From I-15, drive through Hurricane and La Verkin, then east through Virgin, Rockville and Springdale.
evidence.quote: The road descends from this plateau into downtown Hurricane, where SR-59 splits to the south toward the Arizona border. SR-9 then swings north towards the town of La Verkin

evidence.claim: then east through Virgin, Rockville and Springdale.
evidence.quote: After leaving La Verkin, SR-9 heads uphill and passes several mesas before eventually going through the small towns of Virgin, Rockville, and Springdale.

evidence.claim: Inside the park, the road follows the North Fork of the Virgin River before turning up Pine Creek.
evidence.quote: The highway begins on the south side of Zion National Park following along the North Fork of the Virgin River. The road then turns at the junction of Pine Creek and the North Fork of the Virgin River and continues up Pine Creek Canyon

evidence.claim: Beyond the tunnel, continue past Checkerboard Mesa and out the east entrance to US 89 at Mount Carmel Junction.
evidence.quote: Finally the road exits the park through the east entrance and 12 miles (19 km) later ends at the junction of SR-9 and US-89 in Mount Carmel Junction.

evidence.claim: Beyond the tunnel, continue past Checkerboard Mesa
evidence.quote: On the east side of the tunnel the highway continues through impressive scenery, past the Canyon Overlook Trailhead, the East Rim Trailhead and the unique Zion landmark, Checkerboard Mesa.

evidence.claim: Grafton’s farming history includes the work of repeatedly clearing its irrigation ditches.
evidence.quote: Residents had to dredge out clogged irrigation ditches at least weekly, much more often than in most other settlements.

evidence.claim: The settlement began in 1859 as Wheeler, part of Brigham Young’s southern Utah cotton-growing project.
evidence.quote: The site was first settled in December 1859 as part of a southern Utah cotton-growing project ordered by Brigham Young

evidence.claim: The settlement began in 1859 as Wheeler
evidence.quote: A group from Virgin led by Nathan Tenney established a new settlement they called Wheeler.

evidence.claim: The Virgin River flood of 1862 largely destroyed Wheeler, and settlers rebuilt upriver as New Grafton.
evidence.quote: Wheeler didn't last long; it was largely destroyed on the night of January 8, 1862 by a weeks-long flood of the Virgin River, part of the Great Flood of 1862. The rebuilt town, about a mile upriver, was named New Grafton

evidence.claim: Silt clogged the irrigation channels, and continued severe flooding discouraged resettlement.
evidence.quote: Continued severe flooding discouraged resettlement

evidence.claim: Silt clogged the irrigation channels
evidence.quote: One particular challenge to farming was the large amounts of silt in Grafton's section of the Virgin River.

evidence.claim: The Grafton Heritage Partnership formed in 1997 to preserve the townsite; restoration work included the old church and several houses.
evidence.quote: In June 1997, the Grafton Heritage Partnership was organized to protect, preserve, and restore the Grafton Townsite.

evidence.claim: restoration work included the old church and several houses.
evidence.quote: the old church, Russell Home, Louisa Foster Home, the Berry fence in the cemetery, and John Wood home were restored

evidence.claim: Residents had dug canals and planted orchards, some of which survive; the preservation partnership also bought farmland where agriculture continues.
evidence.quote: The community also dug irrigation canals and planted orchards, some of which still exist.

evidence.claim: the preservation partnership also bought farmland where agriculture continues.
evidence.quote: In addition, 150 acres (61 ha) of farmland were purchased, on which agricultural operations are performed to enhance the farming appearance.

evidence.claim: The tunnel follows the canyon wall, keeping its centerline 21 feet from the outer rock face.
evidence.quote: The highway features a 5,613-foot (1,711 m) tunnel that follows the profile of the Pine Creek Canyon wall at a consistent distance of 21 feet (6.4 m) from the outside face of the rock to the centerline of the tunnel.

evidence.claim: Its galleries let in light and air, but also served construction: crews dumped excavated rock through them into the canyon.
evidence.quote: The tunnel uses galleries to provide light and ventilation through the canyon wall to the outside air. The galleries also provided a place to dispose of rock generated during construction, which was dumped through the galleries into the canyon.

evidence.claim: Workers used mining techniques, beginning inside the rock and working outward toward the portals.
evidence.quote: Construction proceeded using mining techniques rather than traditional tunneling techniques, starting from a stope and working outward to the portals.

evidence.claim: The Nevada Construction Company began the tunnel in 1927 and completed it in 1930.
evidence.quote: Work on the tunnel was started in 1927 by the Nevada Construction Company and was completed in 1930

evidence.claim: Parking spaces once provided at the galleries were removed for safety.
evidence.quote: Parking spaces were originally provided at the galleries, but were discontinued due to safety concerns.

evidence.claim: The western portal has a cut-sandstone facade; the eastern opening is shaped to resemble a natural hole and is entered directly from a bridge.
evidence.quote: The west portal is framed by a masonry façade of cut sandstone, while the east portal is a naturalistically formed hole in the rock, entered directly from a bridge.

evidence.claim: The park entrance fee applies even to through traffic.
evidence.quote: The park entrance fee is required to drive through the section in the park even if you’re not stopping.

evidence.claim: Bicycles are prohibited in the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel.
evidence.quote: Cyclists are NOT allowed to ride through the Zion–Mount Carmel Tunnel.

evidence.claim: Two different processes drew the grid on Checkerboard Mesa’s white sandstone.
evidence.quote: The horizontal lines are caused by cross-bedding, a remnant of ancient sand dunes. The vertical and sub-vertical lines formed by the contraction and expansion of the sandstone caused by temperature changes, freezing and thawing cycles, in combination with wetting and drying.

evidence.claim: The horizontal lines preserve cross-bedding from ancient dunes.
evidence.quote: The horizontal lines are caused by cross-bedding, a remnant of ancient sand dunes.

evidence.claim: Vertical and near-vertical lines developed as temperature changes, freezing and thawing, and wetting and drying made the sandstone expand and contract.
evidence.quote: The vertical and sub-vertical lines formed by the contraction and expansion of the sandstone caused by temperature changes, freezing and thawing cycles, in combination with wetting and drying.

evidence.claim: The mesa rises 900 feet above the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway, immediately southwest of the east entrance.
evidence.quote: Checkerboard Mesa is situated immediately southwest of the park's east entrance, towering 900 feet (270 meters) above the Zion – Mount Carmel Highway.

evidence.claim: The name became official in 1935, after park superintendent Preston P. Patraw had called it Checkerboard Mountain.
evidence.quote: This peak was originally named Checkerboard Mountain by the park's third superintendent, Preston P. Patraw. The landform's toponym was officially adopted in 1935 by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names.

evidence.claim: Crazy Quilt Mesa lies half a mile west, across a canyon whose rainwater pools provide water for resident bighorn sheep.
evidence.quote: Its nearest neighbor is Crazy Quilt Mesa, one-half mile immediately west, and separated by Checkerboard Mesa Canyon. This canyon holds pools of rainwater which provide a vital source of water for resident bighorn sheep.

evidence.claim: Horizontal dune bedding crosses vertical weathering lines in the white sandstone.
evidence.quote: The descriptive name stems from the cliff's distinctive multitudinous check lines in cross-bedded white sandstone which give the impression of a checkerboard.

evidence.claim: Horizontal dune bedding crosses vertical weathering lines in the white sandstone.
evidence.quote: The horizontal lines are caused by cross-bedding, a remnant of ancient sand dunes. The vertical and sub-vertical lines formed by the contraction and expansion of the sandstone caused by temperature changes, freezing and thawing cycles, in combination with wetting and drying.
